mainTopic: Collateral and שמיטה, down payments, and whether backing out of a spoken promise counts as מחוסרי אמנה (breaking faith)
overview: The amud opens by finishing a discussion of a ברייתא about a loan backed by a משכון (collateral) worth only half the loan. In it, רבן שמעון בן גמליאל and רבי יהודה הנשיא argue about whether שמיטה cancels such a loan. The גמרא first tries to tie their argument to the dispute over whether a ערבון (down payment) acquires כנגד כולו (the whole deal) or כנגדו (only its own value). It then pushes the link away by saying that, for רבי יהודה הנשיא, the collateral may be only a reminder. Next comes the story of רב כהנא, who was paid in advance for flax. רב ruled that he must deliver only what the money covered, because backing out of mere words is not מחוסרי אמנה (breaking faith). The גמרא presents this as a dispute: רב says spoken promises carry no such problem, and רבי יוחנן says they do. Challenges follow from 'הין צדק', from the curse of 'מי שפרע', and from the story of רבי יוחנן בן מתיא and the hired workers. Then רבי יוחנן's own statements about promised gifts and about a לוי's מעשר are examined. The result is that a small gift, which people rely on, may not be taken back. The amud ends with רבא's ruling on sesame sellers who backed out of a deal, and with the start of a story about an especially honest rabbi, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Then why would the lender bother holding collateral?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the reading in which רבי יהודה הנשיא lets שמיטה cancel even the half of the loan backed by collateral.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if even the covered half is cancelled, why does he need the collateral he is holding?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the idea that, for רבי יהודה הנשיא, שמיטה cancels even the half of the loan that is backed by the משכון. If that were true, why would the lender take collateral at all?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The whole point of taking a משכון seems to be making sure the lender can collect at least something after שמיטה. A reading that makes the collateral useless looks unlikely. So the גמרא will now offer a different reading.

keyTerms.meaning: Collateral, a pledge the lender holds for the loan
Holds, takes
Why does he need it?

phrases.english: But the collateral that he holds, why does he need it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the reading of the ברייתא that the גמרא raised just before this section.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading in which רבי יהודה הנשיא lets שמיטה cancel even the half backed by collateral
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the collateral gives no protection at all, there would be no reason for the lender to take it.

steps.title: A new reading: the dispute is about the whole loan or only half
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא concludes that רבן שמעון בן גמליאל protects the entire loan, while רבי יהודה הנשיא lets שמיטה cancel only the half without collateral.
steps.simpleTranslation: So we must conclude: when רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says 'it does not cancel,' he means none of the loan is cancelled. When רבי יהודה הנשיא says 'it cancels,' he means only the half that has no collateral.
steps.whatsHappening: Since the first reading failed, the גמרא proposes a new one. Both sides agree the covered half is safe. They argue only about the uncovered half.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, the משכון protects the whole loan even though it is worth only half. For רבי יהודה הנשיא, the משכון protects only as much as it is worth, so the other half is cancelled. This keeps the collateral meaningful for both.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, must we not conclude from this?
Cancels (the loan, through שמיטה)
In its entirety
Half

phrases.english: Rather, do we not conclude from it:
What is the meaning of 'it does not cancel'
that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says?
It does not cancel any of the loan,
and what is the meaning of 'it cancels'
that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says?

phrases.aramaic: לְהָךְ פַּלְגָא דְּלָא נָקֵיט עֲלֵיהּ מַשְׁכּוֹן.
phrases.english: It refers to that half for which he does not hold collateral.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a replacement reading after step 1 rejected the earlier one.
steps.raayaObject: That the תנאים disagree about whether collateral protects the entire loan or only its own value
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא about lending against a משכון worth half the loan, read in a way that keeps the collateral meaningful

steps.title: Linking the collateral dispute to the down payment dispute
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says this ברייתא matches the earlier dispute about whether a ערבון acquires the whole sale or only its own value.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this is what they disagree about: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל holds that it acquires against the whole, and רבי יהודה הנשיא holds that it acquires only against its own value.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא connects the dispute between these two תנאים to the earlier argument about a ערבון (down payment). That makes it look like the אמוראים' dispute already appears in a ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A partial collateral is like a partial down payment. Does a part secure the whole, or only its own share? רבן שמעון בן גמליאל holds כנגד כולו, the whole. רבי יהודה הנשיא holds כנגדו, only its own value.

keyTerms.meaning: And this is what they disagree about
It acquires against the whole amount
It acquires only against its own value

steps.whyThisMatters: If this link holds, the later אמוראים who argue about ערבון would be repeating an older dispute between תנאים, and each side would have a תנא to rely on.

phrases.english: And this is what they disagree about,
that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds:
it acquires against the whole,
phrases.notes: This uses the language of the earlier down payment dispute: does a partial payment secure the whole deal?

phrases.english: and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi holds:
it acquires only against its own value.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the reading in step 2 and ties it to the earlier ערבון dispute.
steps.raayaObject: That the dispute among the אמוראים over כנגד כולו versus כנגדו is already a dispute among תנאים
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא as read in step 2

steps.title: No: maybe the dispute is about the covered half
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the link. It says רבן שמעון בן גמליאל protects only the covered half, while רבי יהודה הנשיא cancels even that half.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. When רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says 'it does not cancel,' he means only the half covered by collateral. This shows that רבי יהודה הנשיא holds that even the covered half is cancelled.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on step 3 by offering another way to read the ברייתא. With this reading, the dispute has nothing to do with ערבון.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now both sides agree that the uncovered half is cancelled. They argue only about the covered half. רבי יהודה הנשיא says even that half is cancelled. That brings back the question from step 1: what is the collateral for?

keyTerms.meaning: No. This rejects the previous suggestion
By implication, which shows that
Also, too

steps.confusionAlert: This looks just like the reading that step 1 attacked. The difference is that this time the גמרא will answer the 'why collateral?' question instead of giving up on the reading.

phrases.english: No, what is the meaning of 'it does not cancel'
that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says?
It refers to that half for which he holds collateral,
which shows that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi holds:

phrases.aramaic: לְהָךְ פַּלְגָא דְּנָקֵיט עֲלֵיהּ מַשְׁכּוֹן נָמֵי מְשַׁמֵּט.
phrases.english: even that half for which he holds collateral, it cancels as well.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא, מַאי ״אֵינוֹ מְשַׁמֵּט״ דְּקָאָמַר רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the link to the ערבון dispute made in step 3.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof that the ערבון dispute already appears in this ברייתא
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ברייתא can be read as a dispute about the covered half only, so it does not have to match the כנגד כולו versus כנגדו dispute.

steps.title: The same question returns: why hold collateral?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks again why the lender holds collateral if, for רבי יהודה הנשיא, even the covered half is cancelled.
steps.simpleTranslation: But the collateral he holds, why does he need it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא repeats the question from step 1, now aimed at the new reading in step 4. This time it will give an answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words are the same as in step 1, but now they test whether the new reading can survive. The reading stands only if the collateral has some purpose.

phrases.english: But the collateral that he holds, why does he need it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reading in step 4 by repeating the question from step 1.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יהודה הנשיא's view, as read in step 4, that even the covered half is cancelled
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the collateral gives no protection against שמיטה, taking it seems to serve no purpose.

steps.title: The collateral is just a reminder
steps.stepSummary: The collateral serves only as a reminder of the debt. It does not protect the loan from שמיטה.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is simply a reminder of the matter.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the lender holds the collateral only to remind the borrower of the loan. This saves the reading in step 4.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי יהודה הנשיא, the משכון has no legal power against שמיטה. It works as a practical reminder that pushes the borrower to repay. So the ברייתא does not prove the ערבון dispute.

keyTerms.meaning: A reminder of the matter
Merely, simply

steps.whatToRemember: The attempt to find the ערבון dispute (כנגד כולו versus כנגדו) in the משכון ברייתא is pushed off. You can read רבי יהודה הנשיא as holding that collateral is only a reminder and does not stop שמיטה.

phrases.english: It is merely a reminder of the matter.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 5.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining what the collateral is for
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Collateral must give legal protection, or else no one would take it.
steps.terutzMaskana: Collateral can serve only as a reminder, without any legal effect against שמיטה.

steps.title: רב כהנא's flax deal goes up in price
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא was paid in advance for flax, the price rose, and he went to רב to ask what he must do.
steps.simpleTranslation: People gave רב כהנא money for flax. In the end the price of flax went up. He came before רב.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new story about a sale paid in advance. It sets up a question for רב to answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The buyers paid some money and agreed to a deal at the old price, and the price has now gone up. The question is whether רב כהנא must deliver all the flax he promised or only as much as the money he received covers. This connects to the earlier topic of whether a partial payment secures the whole deal.

keyTerms.meaning: Money (literally, zuzim, a type of coin)
Flax, linen
Became more expensive

phrases.aramaic: רַב כָּהֲנָא יְהַבוּ לֵיהּ זוּזֵי אַכִּיתָּנָא,
phrases.english: People gave Rav Kahana money for flax,
in the end the flax became more expensive.
He came before Rav.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב כָּהֲנָא יְהַבוּ לֵיהּ זוּזֵי אַכִּיתָּנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new practical case on the theme of partial payment.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How much flax רב כהנא must deliver now that the price has gone up

steps.title: רב: deliver for the money received; the rest was only words
steps.stepSummary: רב rules that רב כהנא must deliver flax worth the money he received. Backing out of the rest is not breaking faith, because it was only a verbal promise.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Give them flax for the money you received. The rest is only words, and backing out of words does not count as being someone who breaks faith.
steps.whatsHappening: רב tells רב כהנא to deliver only as much flax as the money he took covers. He adds that backing out of the rest is not considered untrustworthy.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The money acquires only its own share, which fits the כנגדו הוא קונה approach. The remaining agreement was never sealed with money, so it is only דברים, words. Backing out of mere words does not make someone a מחוסר אמנה, a person who breaks faith.

keyTerms.meaning: They are only words, a verbal agreement
The rest, the other part
Lacking trustworthiness, people who break faith

steps.whatToRemember: In רב כהנא's case, the money paid acquires only its own value. Backing out of the rest of the deal, which was only spoken, is not considered breaking faith.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets a practical rule for advance payments when prices change. The money binds both sides only for its own value.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: בְּמַאי דִּנְקִיטַתְּ זוּזֵי – הַב לְהוּ,
phrases.english: He said to him: For what you took money, give them,
phrases.notes: He means: give them as much flax as the money you received pays for, at the old price.

phrases.english: and the rest is only words,

phrases.aramaic: וּדְבָרִים אֵין בָּהֶן מִשּׁוּם מְחוּסְּרֵי אֲמָנָה.
phrases.english: and backing out of words does not count as breaking faith.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: בְּמַאי דִּנְקִיטַתְּ זוּזֵי – הַב לְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: רב answers the question raised by רב כהנא's case in step 7.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Deliver flax for the money received. Backing out of the rest is not breaking faith, because it was only words.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Money acquires only against its own value. Backing out of the unpaid rest is not considered being מחוסר אמנה.

steps.title: רב and רבי יוחנן argue about verbal promises
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא links רב's ruling to a known argument: רב says backing out of a verbal promise is not breaking faith, and רבי יוחנן says it is.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was stated: about words alone, רב says they do not count as breaking faith, and רבי יוחנן says they do count as breaking faith.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that what רב told רב כהנא fits a well-known view of his. It brings the argument between רב and רבי יוחנן about verbal promises.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is about a promise made only in words, with no act that makes the deal binding. רב says backing out is not מחוסרי אמנה. רבי יוחנן says that even without a binding act, backing out is a lack of faithfulness.

keyTerms.meaning: Words alone, a verbal promise with no binding act
People lacking faithfulness, those who break their word

steps.whyThisMatters: This dispute is the backbone of the rest of the sugya. The challenges in steps 10–12 are aimed at רב's lenient view. From step 15 on, the גמרא tests רבי יוחנן's view instead.

phrases.english: As it was stated: regarding words,
phrases.notes: He means a deal agreed on only by talking, with no act that makes it binding.

phrases.english: Rav says: they do not involve
breaking faith,
and Rabbi Yochanan says: they do involve
breaking faith.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows that רב's ruling in Step 8 matches his known position in a dispute with רבי יוחנן.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב: backing out of a verbal promise is not מחוסרי אמנה. רבי יוחנן: it is מחוסרי אמנה.

steps.title: Challenge from 'a just hin'
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא reads the words 'הין צדק' as 'your yes should be honest', which suggests you must keep your word. This is a challenge to רב.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged: רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה says, why does the פסוק say 'a just הין'? Isn't a הין already included in an איפה? Rather, it comes to tell you that your 'yes' should be honest and your 'no' should be honest.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב with a ברייתא that teaches you must keep your yes and your no.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A הין is a smaller measure that is already covered by the איפה, so mentioning it seems extra. רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה reads it as 'הֵן', meaning 'yes', and teaches that a person's word must be reliable. That sounds like backing out of a promise is wrong, which goes against רב.

keyTerms.meaning: A liquid measure, smaller than an איפה
A larger dry measure
Yes

phrases.aramaic: מֵיתִיבִי, רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר:
phrases.english: They challenged: Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda says:
Why does the verse say 'a just hin'?
Wasn't a hin already included in an ephah?
Rather, it is to tell you:
that your 'yes' should be just,
phrases.notes: A play on words: הִין (the measure) sounds like הֵן, 'yes'.

phrases.english: and your 'no' should be just.

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵיתִיבִי, רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רב's position from Step 9.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's view that backing out of a verbal promise is not breaking faith.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the תורה requires your 'yes' to be honest, then going back on a verbal promise should be wrong.

steps.title: אביי: do not say one thing and mean another
steps.stepSummary: אביי explains that the ברייתא only forbids promising something while already planning not to do it.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: that teaching means a person should not say one thing with his mouth and another thing in his heart.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers the challenge by narrowing what 'your yes should be honest' means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק is about honesty at the moment you speak. It forbids promising while secretly planning not to follow through. A person who meant his promise and later changed his mind because things changed, like רב כהנא, has not broken this rule.

keyTerms.meaning: One thing in the mouth and another in the heart

phrases.english: Abaye said: that one
phrases.notes: 'That one' is the teaching of רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה from the step before.

phrases.english: means that he should not say one thing with his mouth
and another thing in his heart.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 10.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the scope of the source
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא requires you to keep every verbal promise.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא only forbids making a promise you never meant to keep. It says nothing against changing your mind later.

steps.title: Challenge from the curse on one who does not keep his word
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון teaches that God will punish whoever does not stand by his word, which seems to go against רב.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged: רבי שמעון says, even though they said a garment acquires a gold dinar but a gold dinar does not acquire a garment, and that is the law, still they said: He Who punished the generation of the flood and the generation of the dispersion will punish whoever does not stand by his word.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second challenge to רב, a strong warning against anyone who does not keep his word.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי שמעון agrees that by law, paying money does not complete the deal, so a person may back out. Even so, he says God punishes someone who goes back on his word. The phrase 'does not stand by his word' sounds like words alone create a real obligation, which goes against רב.

keyTerms.meaning: A garment
A gold coin
He Who punished, a warning that God punishes one who backs out
The generation of the dispersion (the Tower of Bavel)
Stands by his word

phrases.english: They challenged: Rabbi Shimon says:
Even though they said
a garment acquires a gold dinar,
phrases.notes: When one side takes the garment, the deal is done and the other side gets the coin.

phrases.english: but a gold dinar does not acquire a garment,
in any case, that is the law.
But they said: He Who punished
the people of the generation of the flood
and the people of the generation of the dispersion
will in the future punish
whoever does not stand by his word!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second challenge to רב, after אביי answered the first.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's view that backing out of a verbal promise is not breaking faith.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי שמעון condemns anyone who 'does not stand by his word', which implies words alone carry a moral obligation.

steps.title: It is a dispute between תנאים
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that this question is a dispute between תנאים. It begins quoting a story about רבי יוחנן בן מתיא, whose son hired workers and promised them food.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is a dispute between תנאים. As we learned: there was a story with רבי יוחנן בן מתיא, who said to his son, 'Go hire workers for us.' The son went and agreed to give them food.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא does not argue with רבי שמעון. It says other תנאים disagree with him, so רב can follow them. It then starts quoting the source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Instead of explaining רבי שמעון's words differently, the גמרא admits that רבי שמעון holds like רבי יוחנן. רב follows a different תנא. The story is set up here: the son promised food without saying what kind.

keyTerms.meaning: It is a dispute between תנאים
Hired workers
Agreed to give them food

phrases.english: It is a dispute between Tannaim.

phrases.aramaic: דִּתְנַן: מַעֲשֶׂה בְּרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן בֶּן מַתְיָא
phrases.english: As we learned: there was an incident with Rabbi Yochanan ben Matya
who said to his son:
Go out and hire workers for us.
He went and agreed to give them food.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 12 by saying the issue is a dispute between תנאים.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי שמעון's teaching proves that רב is wrong.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי שמעון is only one side of a dispute between תנאים. רב can follow the other side.

steps.title: The father changes the deal before work begins
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן בן מתיא tells his son that an open promise of food could never be fully paid. So the son must go back before the work starts and limit the deal to bread and beans.
steps.simpleTranslation: When he came to his father, his father said: My son, even if you make them a meal like שלמה's feast in his time, you have not fulfilled your duty to them, because they are children of אברהם, יצחק and יעקב. Rather, before they start working, go and tell them: on condition that you may only claim bread and beans from me.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues the quote. The father tells his son to go back and change what he promised before the workers begin.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The son's open promise of 'food' could mean the finest meals, since these workers are children of the אבות. The father lets the son change the verbal deal before any work starts, and that seems to fit רב. The גמרא will explain how this proves the point next.

keyTerms.meaning: The royal feast of King שלמה
You have not fulfilled your duty
On condition that
Bread and beans, a simple standard meal

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the father is being stingy. The point is that an open promise has no limit, so he fixes the terms before work begins, while the deal is still only words.

phrases.english: And when he came to his father, he said to him:
My son, even if you make for them
a meal like the feast of Solomon in his time,
you have not fulfilled your duty to them,
since they are children of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
Rather, before they begin the work,
go out and say to them:
On condition that you have no claim on me
except bread and beans alone.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the source quoted in Step 13, which shows a תנאי view that supports רב.
steps.raayaObject: That some תנאים hold that a verbal agreement may be changed, which fits רב.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה about רבי יוחנן בן מתיא (בבא מציעא 83a), where the father changes the son's verbal deal before work begins.

steps.title: How could the father tell his son to change the deal?
steps.stepSummary: If breaking a spoken promise counts as מחוסרי אמנה, how could רבי יוחנן בן מתיא tell his son to go back on what he promised the workers?
steps.simpleTranslation: If you think that breaking a spoken promise counts as lacking faithfulness, how could the father tell his son, 'Go back on your word'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the story we just learned. A great תנא told his son to change a promise, and that seems to clash with the view that breaking your word is wrong.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The view under attack is that spoken words alone, with no קנין, still carry a moral duty, and breaking them makes you a מחוסר אמנה. Yet in the story the father told his son to go back and limit the promise of food. So either breaking words is allowed, or the story needs another explanation.

keyTerms.meaning: People lacking faithfulness, who break their word
If it enters your mind, meaning if you think so
Go back on your word

phrases.english: And if it enters your mind

phrases.aramaic: דְּבָרִים יֵשׁ בָּהֶן מִשּׁוּם מְחוּסְּרֵי אֲמָנָה,
phrases.english: that spoken words carry the problem of lacking faithfulness,
how did he say to him
'Go back on your word'?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי סָלְקָא דַעְתָּךְ דְּבָרִים יֵשׁ בָּהֶן מִשּׁוּם מְחוּסְּרֵי אֲמָנָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the story quoted in steps 13-14 by setting it against the view that breaking spoken words is wrong.
steps.kashyaTarget: The view that spoken words carry the problem of מחוסרי אמנה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A great תנא told his son to take back a spoken promise, which suggests it is allowed to break your word.

steps.title: The workers never relied on the son
steps.stepSummary: That case is different: the workers knew the son depended on his father's approval, so they never fully relied on his promise.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is different there, because the workers themselves did not rely on it. Why? They knew well that he was relying on his father.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the son was not really breaking trust. The workers knew his promise still needed his father's OK.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The problem of מחוסרי אמנה only applies when the other side truly counted on your words. Here the workers knew the son was acting on his father's behalf, so in their minds the deal was not yet final. Changing it was therefore not a betrayal.

keyTerms.meaning: It is different there
They rely on it; their minds are settled on it
They surely know

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the key idea for the rest of the sugya: whether breaking a promise is wrong depends on whether the other person relied on it.

phrases.english: It is different there,
because the workers themselves
did not rely on it.
What is the reason?
They know well
that he relies on his father.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 15 by showing that the story is a special case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The father allowed his son to break a promise the workers relied on.
steps.terutzMaskana: The workers never relied on the son's promise, so changing it was not a breach of faith.

steps.title: Then why not change the deal even after work began?
steps.stepSummary: If the workers never relied on the son, the son should be able to change the deal even after they started working. Why did the father insist on before?
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, then even if they had already started the work, he could still change it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the answer. The father said to change the deal before the work starts, and that suggests timing matters.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the reason is that the workers knew the son depended on his father, that reason should stay true even after work begins. But the father stressed doing it before they started. So something must change once they begin working.

keyTerms.meaning: If so
They began the work

phrases.english: If so,
even if they began the work, he could change it too?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי, אֲפִילּוּ הִתְחִילוּ בִּמְלָאכָה נָמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 16 using the detail from step 14 that the change had to happen before work began.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that the workers did not rely on the son
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: That reason has nothing to do with timing, yet the father insisted on changing the deal before work started.

steps.title: Once work starts, the workers do rely on him
steps.stepSummary: Once the workers start, they assume the son already checked with his father and got approval, so now they truly rely on the deal.
steps.simpleTranslation: Once they began the work, they certainly rely on it. They say: he surely told his father, and his father is fine with it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why timing matters. Starting work makes the workers assume the father approved, so from then on they count on the promise.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before work starts, the deal still looks uncertain because the father has not weighed in. Once they begin, the workers assume the son already got his father's OK. Now they rely on it, so changing it would be a real breach of faith.

keyTerms.meaning: Certainly
He surely said
It is fine with him; he agrees

steps.whatToRemember: The story of רבי יוחנן בן מתיא does not prove you may break a promise. The son could change the deal only before the workers began, because only then did they not yet rely on it.

phrases.english: Once they began the work,
they certainly rely on it,
for they say:
He surely said it before his father
and it is fine with him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 17.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing between before and after the work begins
steps.terutzHavaAmina: If the workers did not rely on the son, timing should not matter.
steps.terutzMaskana: Starting work makes the workers assume the father approved, so from then on they rely on the promise.

steps.title: Did רבי יוחנן really say that?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא questions whether רבי יוחנן holds that breaking your word is wrong, since he taught that someone who promises a gift can take it back.
steps.simpleTranslation: Did רבי יוחנן really say this? But רבה בר בר חנה said in the name of רבי יוחנן: someone who tells his friend 'I am giving you a gift' can go back on it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new challenge. It sets the view that breaking spoken words is wrong against another statement of רבי יוחנן about promised gifts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier on the דף, רבי יוחנן was quoted as holding that spoken words carry the problem of מחוסרי אמנה. Here רבה בר בר חנה quotes him as saying a promised gift can be taken back. These two quotes seem to contradict each other.

keyTerms.meaning: And did he really say?
But didn't he say?
A gift
To go back on it, to take it back

phrases.english: And did Rabbi Yochanan say this?
But didn't Rabba bar bar Chana say
that Rabbi Yochanan said:
One who says to his friend,
'I am giving you a gift,'
can go back on it.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן הָכִי? וְהָאָמַר רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the story to a contradiction between two statements of רבי יוחנן.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוחנן's view that spoken words carry the problem of מחוסרי אמנה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Another quote from רבי יוחנן says a promised gift may be taken back, so breaking spoken words would be fine.

steps.title: 'Can' must mean 'is allowed'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that 'he can go back' must mean 'he is allowed to go back,' since he obviously is able to.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'He can'? That is obvious! Rather, it means he is permitted to go back on it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pauses to clarify the word 'can' in רבי יוחנן's statement. This sharpens the challenge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Without a קנין, nobody can force the giver to hand over the gift, so saying he is 'able' to go back would teach nothing. So רבי יוחנן must mean it is morally allowed. That makes the clash with מחוסרי אמנה much stronger.

keyTerms.meaning: Obvious
Rather
Permitted

steps.confusionAlert: Do not read 'יכול' as 'is able' here. The גמרא makes clear it means 'is allowed,' and the whole challenge depends on that.

phrases.english: 'He can'? That is obvious!
phrases.notes: No one can force him to give a gift he never formally handed over.

phrases.english: Rather, it means he is permitted to go back on it.

steps.triggerLanguage: יָכוֹל, פְּשִׁיטָא! אֶלָּא: מוּתָּר לַחֲזוֹר בּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Clarifies the wording of the source quoted in step 19, which sharpens the קשיא.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What does 'יכול לחזור בו' mean if he is obviously able to go back?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: It means he is permitted to go back, with no breach of faith.

steps.title: A small gift is different
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא answers that רבי יוחנן agrees that a small gift may not be taken back, because people do rely on it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: רבי יוחנן agrees about a small gift, because people rely on it.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא settles the contradiction. רבי יוחנן's permission to take back a gift applies to a big gift, but not to a small one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Again, the key question is whether the other person relied on the promise. People do not fully count on a large promised gift, so taking it back is allowed. A small gift they do count on, so taking it back would be מחוסרי אמנה.

keyTerms.meaning: And he agrees
A small gift

steps.whatToRemember: According to רב פפא, רבי יוחנן holds that a promised large gift may be taken back, but a promised small gift may not, because people rely on it.
steps.whyThisMatters: This becomes the practical rule: whether you may back out of a spoken promise depends on whether the other person was expected to rely on it.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
And Rabbi Yochanan agrees
about a small gift,
because people rely on it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: וּמוֹדֶה רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן בְּמַתָּנָה מוּעֶטֶת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in steps 19-20.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (small gift versus large gift)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי יוחנן allows taking back any promised gift.
steps.terutzMaskana: He allows it only for a large gift. A small gift is relied on, so it may not be taken back.

steps.title: Proof from the לוי and the מעשר
steps.stepSummary: Another teaching of רבי יוחנן, about a לוי told he has a כור of מעשר, shows that in some cases he holds a promise may not be taken back.
steps.simpleTranslation: This makes sense, because רבי אבהו said in the name of רבי יוחנן: if a ישראל tells a לוי, 'You have a כור of מעשר with me,' the לוי may use it as תרומת מעשר for his produce somewhere else. That works if the ישראל cannot go back on his word. But if he could, why would it be allowed? The לוי might end up eating טבל!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings support for רב פפא's answer. Another ruling of רבי יוחנן only makes sense if the ישראל is not allowed to take back his promise.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The לוי is relying completely on the ישראל's spoken promise, using that מעשר to fix his other produce. If the ישראל were allowed to take it back, the לוי's separation would fail and his other produce would stay טבל. So רבי יוחנן must hold that here the promise cannot be taken back, which fits רב פפא's idea that some promises are relied on and must be kept.

keyTerms.meaning: So too it is logical; this supports the idea
The tenth of produce given to a לוי
The tenth the לוי must separate from his מעשר and give to a כהן
Allowed
Untithed produce, which may not be eaten
It turns out

phrases.english: So too it is logical,
for Rabbi Abahu said
that Rabbi Yochanan said:
An Israelite who said to a Levite,
'You have a kor of tithe in my hands' —
phrases.notes: A כור is a large measure of grain. He means he set aside מעשר for this לוי.

phrases.english: the Levite is allowed to make it
the teruma of the tithe for produce in another place.
It works well if you say
that he cannot go back on it —
that is why the Levite is allowed.
But if you say
that he can go back on it,
why is the Levite allowed?
It would turn out that he is eating untithed produce!
phrases.notes: If the ישראל takes it back, the לוי separated from food that wasn't his, so his other produce was never fixed.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָכִי נָמֵי מִסְתַּבְּרָא, דְּאָמַר רַבִּי אֲבָהוּ אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רב פפא's answer from step 21 with another teaching of רבי יוחנן.
steps.raayaObject: רב פפא's claim that רבי יוחנן agrees some promised gifts may not be taken back
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי אבהו in the name of רבי יוחנן: a לוי told he has a כור of מעשר may use it as תרומת מעשר for other produce, which only works if the ישראל cannot go back on his word

steps.title: Maybe the לוי already took the produce
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes away the proof from רבי יוחנן's לוי case. It suggests the case is where the לוי already took the מעשר and then left it with the owner for safekeeping.
steps.simpleTranslation: Here we are dealing with a case where the לוי took the produce from the owner and then deposited it back with him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is pushing back on the proof from step 22. It says the לוי case might not be about a mere promise at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the לוי had already taken the produce, it already belongs to him. Then the owner cannot back out simply because the produce is not his anymore. That would have nothing to do with keeping one's word, so the proof would fall away.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Here, what case are we dealing with?' This is used to narrow a teaching to a specific situation.
He took it (the לוי took the produce)
He deposited it, leaving it with someone for safekeeping

phrases.english: Here, with what are we dealing?
For example, where he took it from him
phrases.notes: 'He' is the לוי, and 'him' is the owner of the produce.

phrases.english: and then deposited it back with him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Pushes away the proof brought in step 22 by narrowing the case.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the proof from the לוי case, not the idea that breaking your word is wrong.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed it was only a spoken promise. It may instead be produce the לוי already owns.

steps.title: The end of the ruling doesn't fit that reading
steps.stepSummary: The end of the same teaching says that if the owner gave the produce to another לוי, the first לוי has only a grievance. That cannot fit a case where the first לוי already owned the produce.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, look at the end of the ruling: if he gave it to a different לוי, the first one has only a grievance against him. But if you think the first לוי took it and deposited it back, why does he have only a grievance? Once he pulled it into his possession, it is his property in the owner's hands!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the suggestion from step 23. It uses the second half of the same ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the first לוי had already acquired the produce, giving it to someone else would be like taking his property. He could then sue to get it back. He would not have 'only a grievance.' So the case cannot be one where he already took it.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Say the end clause.' The גמרא checks the later part of the same teaching.
A grievance, a moral complaint with no legal claim
He pulled it, a way of acquiring movable objects (מְשִׁיכָה)
If it enters your mind, if you were to think

phrases.english: If so, say the latter clause:
If he gave it to a different לוי,
he has nothing against him but a grievance.
And if it enters your mind
that it is where he took it from him
and then deposited it with him,

phrases.aramaic: אַמַּאי אֵין לוֹ עָלָיו אֶלָּא תַּרְעוֹמֶת?
phrases.english: why does he have only a grievance against him?
Once he pulled it into his possession,
he has money (property) with him!
phrases.notes: The produce already belongs to the first לוי, so he could demand it back by law.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the case suggested in step 23.
steps.kashyaTarget: The suggestion that the לוי already took the produce and deposited it back
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the לוי owned it, he would have a real legal claim. That contradicts the ruling that he has 'only a grievance.'

steps.title: So the לוי never took it: the proof stands
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא concludes that the לוי case is where nothing was taken. It was only a promise, so backing out of a promise is wrong.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, must we not learn from this that it is a case where he did not take it? Yes, learn from it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא wraps up the back-and-forth. The לוי had only been promised the produce, so the proof from step 22 stands.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the first לוי has only a grievance, he never owned the produce. Yet רבי יוחנן still holds that backing out deserves complaint. This shows that even a spoken promise should be kept, at least where people rely on it.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, is it not so...? This introduces the only remaining option.
Learn from it, a confirmed conclusion

steps.whatToRemember: רבי יוחנן's לוי case is about a promise only, with nothing taken. Still, backing out earns a grievance, so breaking your word is considered bad faith.

phrases.english: Rather, must we not learn from it
that it is where he did not take it?
Learn from it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the conclusion forced by the challenge in step 24.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The לוי case is a mere promise, so רבי יוחנן holds that breaking a reliable promise is wrong.

steps.title: The sesame sellers who backed out
steps.stepSummary: A man paid for sesame. The price rose, the sellers backed out and told him to take his money, he didn't, and the money was stolen.
steps.simpleTranslation: A man paid money for sesame. Then the price of sesame went up. The sellers backed out and told him, 'We have no sesame; take your money.' He didn't take his money, and it was stolen. They came to רבא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a real case to set up רבא's ruling in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two issues are mixed here. First, the sellers backed out of a paid deal. Second, the money stayed with them and was then stolen. The question is whether the sellers must answer for the stolen money.

keyTerms.meaning: Sesame seeds
It became more expensive
They backed out of the deal
It was stolen

phrases.english: A certain man gave money for sesame.
In the end, sesame went up in price.
They backed out and said to him:
We have no sesame; take your money.
He did not take his money; it was stolen.
They came before רבא.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new real-life case about backing out of a deal.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sets up the case: sellers backed out, the buyer left his money with them, and it was stolen.

steps.title: רבא: the sellers aren't even unpaid watchmen
steps.stepSummary: רבא rules that once the sellers told the buyer to take his money, they are not responsible for it at all. They are not even unpaid watchmen.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to the buyer: Since they told you 'take your money' and you didn't, it goes without saying they aren't paid watchmen over it. They aren't even unpaid watchmen.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives his ruling: the sellers do not have to pay for the stolen money.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An unpaid watchman (שומר חנם) still pays if he was careless. רבא says the sellers are not even that, because they told the buyer to take his money. Leaving it with them was the buyer's own choice, so they owe nothing even if they were careless.

keyTerms.meaning: A paid watchman, who pays even for theft
An unpaid watchman, who pays only if careless
It goes without saying, it is not even needed to say

phrases.english: He said to him:
Since they said to you, 'Take your money,'
and you did not take it,

phrases.aramaic: לָא מִבַּעְיָא שׁוֹמֵר שָׂכָר דְּלָא הָוֵי,
phrases.english: it goes without saying that they are not a paid watchman,

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא אֲפִילּוּ שׁוֹמֵר חִנָּם נָמֵי לָא הָוֵי.
phrases.english: but even an unpaid watchman they are not.

steps.triggerLanguage: כֵּיוָן דְּאָמְרִי לָךְ שְׁקוֹל זוּזָךְ וְלָא שְׁקַלְיתְּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the ruling on the case told in step 26.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Once the buyer was told to take his money and didn't, the sellers bear no responsibility for it at all.

steps.title: But what about the curse of 'מי שפרע'?
steps.stepSummary: The rabbis object: even if the sellers owe nothing for the theft, didn't they back out of a paid deal? Then they must accept the curse of 'מי שפרע.'
steps.simpleTranslation: The rabbis said to רבא: But don't the sellers have to accept upon themselves the curse of 'He Who exacted payment'?
steps.whatsHappening: The rabbis challenge רבא. Not paying for the theft is one thing, but backing out of a paid deal has its own consequence.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The money was paid, so backing out of the deal brings the curse of 'מי שפרע.' The rabbis want to know whether רבא's ruling lets the sellers off from that too. Their challenge separates two things: owing for the stolen money, and the wrong of backing out.

keyTerms.meaning: 'He Who exacted payment,' the curse said to one who backs out of a deal after money was paid
To accept upon himself

phrases.english: The rabbis said to רבא:
But don't they need to accept upon themselves 'He Who exacted payment'?
phrases.notes: This is the curse that God, Who punished earlier generations, will punish someone who does not keep his word.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא בָּעֵי לְקַבּוֹלֵי עֲלֵיהּ מִי שֶׁפָּרַע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges whether רבא's ruling fully clears the sellers.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's ruling that the sellers are free of all liability
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Backing out after money was paid normally requires accepting the curse of 'מי שפרע.'

steps.title: רבא agrees: they must accept the curse
steps.stepSummary: רבא agrees that the sellers must accept the curse of 'מי שפרע' for backing out.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to them: Yes, that is so.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא accepts the rabbis' point. The sellers owe nothing for the stolen money, but they still face the curse for backing out of the deal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His ruling about the theft stays in place. He simply adds that the moral wrong of backing out after payment still earns the curse.

keyTerms.meaning: Indeed so, an agreement with the questioner

steps.whatToRemember: The sellers are not responsible for the stolen money because they told him to take it. Yet backing out of a paid deal still brings the curse of 'מי שפרע.'

phrases.english: He said to them: Indeed so.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 28 by agreeing with it.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Concession: the challenge is accepted without taking back the earlier ruling
steps.terutzHavaAmina: One might think רבא freed the sellers from every consequence.
steps.terutzMaskana: They are free from paying for the theft but must accept 'מי שפרע.'

steps.title: A rabbi who never changed his word
steps.stepSummary: רב פפי reports through רבינא about a rabbi, named רב טבות or רב שמואל בר זוטרא. This rabbi would never change his word even for all the world.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפי said: רבינא told me that one of the rabbis told him something. His name was רב טבות, and some say רב שמואל בר זוטרא. He was someone who would not change his word even if they gave him the whole world.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a story. First it introduces the speaker and how honest he was.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The speaker's honesty is stressed so we will trust the story that follows. The story itself starts in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: The whole space of the world
Change his word, deviate from what he says

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב פַּפֵּי, אָמַר לִי רָבִינָא:
phrases.english: רב פפי said: רבינא said to me:
To me said a certain one of the rabbis
and רב טבות is his name,

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמְרִי לַהּ רַב שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר זוּטְרָא שְׁמֵיהּ,
phrases.english: and some say רב שמואל בר זוטרא is his name,
who, if they would give him
the whole space of the world,
would not change his word.

steps.title: A man comes asking to buy sesame
steps.stepSummary: The honest rabbi tells his story. Late on a Friday afternoon, a man came to his door and asked if he had sesame to sell.
steps.simpleTranslation: It happened to me. That day was late Friday afternoon, and I was sitting, and a man came and stood at the door. He said to me: Do you have sesame to sell?
steps.whatsHappening: The story begins. The scene is being set, and the story continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: So far nothing has been agreed. A buyer is only asking whether sesame is for sale. This is the setup for whatever the rabbi will say and how he keeps his word.
